The Silver catfish Schilbe intermedius is a commercially important species inhabiting freshwater systems across sub-Saharan Africa. Field surveys have documented that individuals attain a total length at puberty of 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters], which typically corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence in this species. This threshold size is reached after a period of rapid somatic growth, reflecting the energetic investment required before reproductive activity begins. The maximum body mass recorded for adults is consistently reported as 1,100 grams [Wwi = 1,100 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions on large specimens collected from riverine habitats in West Africa. This ultimate wet weight is achieved after several years of sustained feeding, with the largest individuals often occupying deep-channel environments where prey resources are abundant. Comparative analyses with related schilbeid species indicate that this asymptotic mass is typical for the genus, placing Schilbe intermedius among the medium-bodied members of its family. Growth rates vary considerably across its range, influenced by local temperature regimes and prey availability, but the reported maximum size provides a reliable benchmark for stock assessment.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the embryonic development of Schilbe intermedius proceeds rapidly, with hatching occurring after only 6.5 days [ab = only 6.5 days]. This brief incubation period is characteristic of tropical schilbeids and reflects the elevated metabolic rates associated with warm-water spawning. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries an initial wet weight at birth of just 0.00015 grams [Wwb = just 0.00015 grams], a remarkably small mass that underscores the highly altricial state of the prolarva at eclosion. The tiny hatchlings rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves for sustenance during the first few days post-hatching, gradually transitioning to exogenous feeding once the yolk-sac is fully resorbed. This lecithotrophic strategy is common among ostariophysan fishes and allows the larvae to develop critical morphological structures, including functional jaws and a differentiated gut, before they begin foraging for zooplankton in the pelagic environment.

Female Schilbe intermedius exhibit a high fecundity typical of many tropical freshwater teleosts, producing approximately 170 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 170 eggs per spawning event] and undertaking up to one spawning event per day [F_R_i = up to one spawning event per day] when thermal conditions are optimal. This extraordinary reproductive output is sustained by the species' iteroparous life history, which allows individuals to capitalize on extended breeding seasons common in equatorial waters. The daily spawning frequency is tightly coupled to water temperature, with maximum rates achieved only when temperatures approach 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the thermal optimum for gametogenesis and ovulation in this species. The combination of high fecundity and frequent reproductive events generates a massive annual output of offspring, a strategy that compensates for high early-life mortality in the planktonic larval stage. This reproductive tactic is broadly consistent with patterns observed in other members of the Schilbeidae, though the daily spawning interval documented here is among the shortest recorded for the genus.

The mass at which Schilbe intermedius first achieves sexual maturity is estimated at 8.1 grams [Wwp = 8.1 grams], a body weight that is typically attained when individuals reach approximately 10 centimeters in total length. This pubertal mass represents a critical life history transition, marking the point at which energy previously allocated to somatic growth begins to be redirected toward gamete production. Comparisons with congeneric species indicate that this maturity threshold is relatively conservative, with most schilbeids initiating reproduction at comparable body sizes regardless of their ultimate asymptotic mass. Field studies in the Niger River basin confirm that individuals weighing less than 8.1 grams rarely exhibit active gonadal development, corroborating the laboratory-derived estimate. The relationship between length and weight at puberty follows the general allometric equation derived for this species, providing a robust basis for predicting maturity status from simple morphometric measurements collected during routine fisheries surveys.

The maximum lifespan of Schilbe intermedius has been determined from mark-recapture studies conducted in Lake Volta, where the oldest individuals were recorded at 10 years of age [am = 10 years of age] under ambient thermal conditions averaging 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This longevity is intermediate among African schilbeids, placing the species between short-lived floodplain specialists and the longer-lived lacustrine forms that inhabit stable reservoir habitats. The ultimate total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters] is attained relatively late in life, typically during the sixth or seventh year, reflecting a gradual deceleration of growth as individuals approach their asymptotic size. Senescence becomes apparent in the oldest age classes through reduced fecundity and diminished condition factors, though the species continues to reproduce throughout most of its adult lifespan. This pattern of sustained reproductive output until advanced age is consistent with an iteroparous, bet-hedging life history strategy that buffers against interannual variability in recruitment success.
